vision_features.image_context: Close-up photograph of broad, oval-shaped leaves, likely from a leguminous plant. Two to three leaves are visible; the central/foreground leaf is in focus and shows the upper surface. The leaves have visible fine white hairs along the margins and veins. A small curled or rolled portion of leaf tissue is visible at the right edge of the main leaf.
vision_features.abnormalities: 1. Scattered small to medium circular-to-irregular marks across the upper leaf surface: these appear as yellow-green to bright yellow areas, roughly 3–8 mm each, distributed across the central and lower portions of the main leaf. Within or adjacent to many of these yellow areas are dark reddish-brown to near-black spots or clumps, roughly 1–4 mm, with no clearly defined raised structures visible at this resolution. Borders between yellow and green tissue are diffuse. 2. Along the leaf margin (edge), there are larger angular to irregular areas of dark reddish-brown to brown dry-looking tissue, each roughly 5–15 mm, confined primarily to the right and lower margins of the main leaf. These margin areas appear slightly shrunken or puckered. Some of these marginal marks have a yellow-green transitional zone between the dark tissue and the healthy green interior. 3. A portion of the right leaf margin appears torn or missing, creating a ragged edge, and the small curled tissue at the tip-right area shows dark brown discoloration. 4. On the partially visible leaf at lower-left, similar yellow patches with dark brown centers are present, along with what appears to be tan-to-brown dry tissue at the very base of that leaf. 5. Fine white hairs are visible on the leaf surface and margins, appearing normal in texture and distribution.
vision_features.absences: 1. No powdery or dusty white/gray coating is visible on any part of the leaf surfaces. 2. No raised pustules, blister-like bumps, or thread-like growths are visible on the underside (underside is not shown, but the visible surface has none). 3. No wet, slimy, or water-soaked appearance to any of the marks — all affected areas appear dry. 4. No large-scale uniform yellowing of the entire leaf blade; the background green tissue between marks appears healthy in color.
vision_features.summary: The main leaf displays two types of visual abnormalities: scattered small yellow-green spots with dark reddish-brown centers distributed across the blade interior, and larger angular dark brown dry areas concentrated along the leaf margins. The transition zones between affected and healthy tissue often show a yellow-green intermediate color. The leaf margin is the most severely affected area, with dry, darkened tissue and some physical distortion or tearing. The most striking feature is the combination of bright yellow halos surrounding dark brown interior spots scattered across an otherwise green leaf surface.

trace.result_text:
Available classes in 'Soybean_Diseases' (5 total):
   1. Bacterial_Blight
   2. Diaporthe
   3. Green_stem_disorder
   4. Phomopsis
   5. Phytophthora

Knowledge-base entry for 'Bacterial_Blight':
────────────────────────────────────────
Infections begin as small, angular, water-soaked spots that turn yellow and then brown as the tissue dies. Lesions have dark reddish-brown centers surrounded by yellowish-green halos around water-soaked tissue; lesions may coalesce to form large, irregularly shaped lesions. Leaf veins may become affected creating necrotic areas resembling lightning on the leaf. Eventually lesions fall out leaving ragged foliage.. Presence of a yellowish-green halo around lesions; most common on young leaves in mid to upper canopy whereas brown spot is usually seen on older, lower leaves; lack of fungal structures in lesions.. Septoria brown spot, brown spot
────────────────────────────────────────

Knowledge-base entry for 'Diaporthe':
────────────────────────────────────────
Parallel rows of black, flask-shaped specks or pycnidia on mature soybean stems occurring later in the season (R6 to R8 growth stages). Pycnidia may also develop on dry, poorly developed pods, but may be dispersed randomly rather than arranged linearly.. Parallel rows of black, flask-shaped pycnidia arranged linearly on stems; random dispersal on pods.
────────────────────────────────────────

Knowledge-base entry for 'Phomopsis':
────────────────────────────────────────
Infected seed are cracked, shriveled, dull, and may have a gray mold on them.. Seed infected by pod and stem blight may decompose after harvest and have low viability; seedlings grown from infected seeds may often be blighted.
────────────────────────────────────────

Knowledge-base entry for 'Phytophthora':
────────────────────────────────────────
Young plants show rapid yellowing and wilting with soft rot and collapse of the root. Mature plants exhibit general yellowing of lower leaves progressing upward, followed by wilting and death, with brown discolored roots and a dark chocolate-brown stem discoloration extending from below the soil line upward several nodes; leaves typically stay attached after plant death.. The best diagnostic symptom on susceptible varieties is a lower stem discoloration (dark chocolate-brown) that may extend several nodes up the stem. Root system shows lateral and branch roots almost completely discolored; tap roots with brown surface discoloration and tan to brown inner tissue discoloration. Leaves turn yellow, wilt, and typically stay attached after plant death.. stem canker, Pythium
────────────────────────────────────────

Knowledge-base entry for 'Green_stem_disorder':
────────────────────────────────────────
All or part of the soybean plant remains green while the rest of the plant or neighboring plants mature, most commonly seen in stems, leaves or pods; stems remain moist while pods and seeds have ripened.. Stems and occasionally leaves remain green and moist after pods and seeds have ripened and turned brown; excessive leaves on plant and green stems when neighboring plants are near harvest maturity.
────────────────────────────────────────

DISCRIMINATING: 'Bacterial_Blight' vs 'Phytophthora'
Ruling feature : Leaf lesions with yellowish-green halos (Disease A) vs. dark chocolate-brown stem discoloration from soil line upward with root rot (Disease B)
Bacterial_Blight: Angular, water-soaked leaf spots with dark reddish-brown centers surrounded by yellowish-green halos; lesions may coalesce and fall out leaving ragged foliage, with necrotic vein patterns resembling lightning.
Phytophthora: Dark chocolate-brown stem discoloration extending from below the soil line upward several nodes, accompanied by brown discolored roots and general yellowing/wilting with leaves remaining attached after plant death.
Decision rule  : IF the primary symptoms are on leaves as angular lesions with distinct yellowish-green halos, THEN suspect Bacterial Blight (Disease A); IF the primary symptoms are dark chocolate-brown stem discoloration at/below the soil line with root rot and upward wilting, THEN suspect Phytophthora (Disease B).

DISCRIMINATING: 'Bacterial_Blight' vs 'Diaporthe'
Ruling feature : Presence of black flask-shaped pycnidia (fungal structures) on stems vs. water-soaked angular leaf lesions with yellowish-green halos
Bacterial_Blight: Angular, water-soaked leaf spots with dark reddish-brown centers surrounded by yellowish-green halos; lesions may coalesce and fall out leaving ragged foliage, with no fungal structures present.
Diaporthe: Black, flask-shaped pycnidia (fungal structures) arranged in parallel linear rows on mature stems, and randomly on pods; appears late in season (R6–R8 growth stages).
Decision rule  : IF you observe black flask-shaped pycnidia in parallel rows on stems or pods, THEN diagnose Diaporthe; IF you observe angular leaf lesions with yellowish-green halos and water-soaked tissue but NO fungal structures, THEN diagnose Bacterial Blight.
